# Infertility

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Obstetrics/gynecology > Fertility, contraception, and reproductive endocrinology > Infertility*

[Original Article Link](/library/RM0log)

---

## Summary

Infertility is the inability to achieve <u>pregnancy</u> after 12 months of regular unprotected sexual intercourse in female individuals < 35 years of age and after 6 months in those ≥ 35 years of age, or the need for <u>medically assisted reproduction</u> to achieve <u>pregnancy</u>. Causes of <u>female infertility</u> include <u>diminished ovarian reserve</u>, <u>ovulatory dysfunction</u>, and tubal, <u>pelvic</u>, uterine, and cervical disorders. Causes of <u>male infertility</u> include <u>male hypogonadism</u> and <u>sperm</u> transport disorders. Diagnosis involves assessing both partners to determine the underlying causes and typically includes <u>hormone</u> tests to assess ovulatory function, imaging to evaluate for uterine abnormalities and tubal patency, and <u>semen analysis</u>. Management includes treatment of the underlying cause and often <u>medically assisted reproduction</u>, including <u>ovulation induction</u>, <u>intrauterine insemination</u>, and <u>assisted reproductive technology</u> (e.g., <u>in vitro fertilization</u>).

---

## Definitions

* Infertility is characterized by: [[1]](/library/q6dCNI0)

* An inability to achieve <u>pregnancy</u> despite regular unprotected sexual intercourse; based on factors such as age and medical, sexual, and reproductive history

* In female patients < 35 years of age: after 12 months

* In female patients ≥ 35 years of age: after 6 months

* The need for <u>medically assisted reproduction</u> to achieve <u>pregnancy</u>

* Primary infertility: infertility in individuals who have never achieved <u>pregnancy</u> [[2]](/library/nkd7oJ0)

* Secondary infertility: infertility in individuals who have previously achieved at least one <u>pregnancy</u> [[2]](/library/nkd7oJ0)

* Diminished ovarian reserve: : a decline in the number of functioning <u>oocytes</u> (either as a normal consequence of age or due to an underlying disorder such as <u>endometriosis</u>) that manifests as a reduced response to ovarian stimulation in reproductive-aged women with regular <u>menstruation</u> [[3]](/library/yKddQI0)[[4]](/library/5mdiTq0)[[5]](/library/IudYs70)

---

## Etiology

### <u>Female infertility</u>




* <u>Diminished ovarian reserve</u>

* <u>Ovulatory dysfunction</u>

* Tubal/<u>pelvic</u> causes

* <u>Pelvic inflammatory disease</u>

* Blocked or damaged <u>fallopian tubes</u> (e.g., <u>pelvic</u> adhesions, obstruction)

* <u>Endometriosis</u>

* Uterine causes

* <u>Uterine leiomyoma</u>

* <u>Endometrial polyps</u>

* <u>Bicornuate uterus</u>

* <u>Septate uterus</u>

* <u>Asherman syndrome</u>

* <u>Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome</u>

* Cervical causes

* Trauma (e.g., following <u>cryotherapy</u>, <u>conization</u>)

* Immune factors (e.g., <u>antisperm antibodies</u> in the cervical mucus)

* <u>Diethylstilbestrol</u> exposure in utero

* Cervical anomalies (e.g., insufficient cervical mucus production)





### <u>Male infertility</u>




* <u>Hypogonadism</u>; see “<u>Etiology of male hypogonadism</u>.”

* <u>Sperm</u> transport disorders





#### <u>Sperm</u> transport disorders




* Obstructive azoospermia

* Absence of spermatozoa in semen despite normal <u>spermatogenesis</u> due to structural or functional abnormalities (e.g., obstruction, absence, dysfunction) along the <u>sperm</u> transport system (<u>epididymis</u>, <u>vas deferens</u>, <u>ejaculatory duct</u>)

* Possible causes include infection (e.g., <u>gonorrhea</u>), iatrogeny (e.g., due to <u>vasectomy</u>), congenital (e.g., absent <u>vas deferens</u> in patients with <u>cystic fibrosis</u>), or genetic conditions (e.g., decreased <u>sperm</u> motility in <u>primary ciliary dyskinesia</u>).

* <u>Sexual dysfunction</u>

* Anejaculation

* <u>Premature ejaculation</u>





> [!TIP]
> The cause of infertility remains unexplained in up to a third of affected couples. [[7]](/library/_Ed5y70)[[8]](/library/OMdIKq0)

---

## Diagnosis

### General principles [[4]](/library/5mdiTq0)[[5]](/library/IudYs70)[[9]](/library/R5dlPq0)




* Begin initial evaluation for infertility if <u>pregnancy</u> is not achieved after regular unprotected sexual intercourse for at least:

* 12 months in female individuals < 35 years of age

* 6 months in female individuals ≥ 35 years of age

* Refer promptly to a reproductive endocrinologist for evaluation for the following indications: [[10]](/library/k6dmOI0)

* Female individuals > 40 years of age [[11]](/library/I6dYmI0)

* Known or suspected <u>male infertility</u>

* Known or suspected <u>causes of infertility</u>

* <u>Assisted reproductive technology</u> is required or desired (e.g., same-sex couples, individuals with <u>anomalies of the female genital tract</u> such as <u>Mullerian agenesis</u>)

* Evaluate both partners simultaneously to prevent unnecessary studies. [[9]](/library/R5dlPq0)

* Obtain a complete personal and <u>family history</u> of both partners, including:

* Comprehensive <u>gynecologic and obstetric history</u> for female individuals

* Reproductive history (e.g., coital frequency and timing)

* <u>Medical history</u> (e.g., chronic conditions, childhood illness, <u>sexual dysfunction</u>)

* Medication history (e.g., <u>teratogens</u>) and exposures (e.g., smoking, <u>alcohol</u>)

* In patients with <u>amenorrhea</u>:  Perform <u>diagnostics for amenorrhea</u> (e.g., <u>TSH</u> and <u>prolactin</u>) before pursuing <u>infertility workup</u>. [[4]](/library/5mdiTq0)

---

## Female individuals

### Initial assessment [[2]](/library/nkd7oJ0)[[4]](/library/5mdiTq0)[[5]](/library/IudYs70)




#### Approach




* Perform <u>physical examination</u>, including: [[4]](/library/5mdiTq0)

* <u>Skin examination</u> (e.g., for <u>hirsutism</u>, <u>acne</u>, <u>acanthosis nigricans</u>)

* <u>Thyroid examination</u>

* <u>Breast examination</u> (e.g., for tenderness, mass, <u>nipple discharge</u>)

* <u>Speculum examination</u>

* Evaluate for <u>ovulatory dysfunction</u>.

* Patients with <u>amenorrhea</u>, <u>AUB</u>, and/or <u>hirsutism</u>: Perform <u>ovulation</u> testing.

* If no <u>ovulation</u>: Evaluate for underlying cause, i.e., with <u>diagnostics for amenorrhea</u>.

* If <u>ovulation</u> present: Proceed to imaging.

* All other patients: Assume regular <u>ovulation</u> and evaluate for structural pathology with diagnostic imaging.

* Abnormal imaging: Refer to gynecology.

* Normal imaging: Refer to reproductive <u>endocrinology</u> for further assessment (e.g., <u>ovarian reserve testing</u>).





#### <u>Ovulation</u> tests




Options include:




* <u>Ovulation prediction test</u> to identify pending <u>ovulation</u>

* Mid-<u>luteal phase</u> serum <u>progesterone</u> level (∼ 1 week before expected <u>menstrual period</u>)  [[2]](/library/nkd7oJ0)[[4]](/library/5mdiTq0)[[12]](/library/O6dIOI0)

* â¥ 3 ng/mL: suggests <u>ovulation</u> has recently occurred

* < 3 ng/mL: suggests <u>anovulation</u>

* Mid-<u>luteal phase</u> <u>transvaginal ultrasound</u> to evaluate quantity and size of developing follicles





#### Imaging




* <u>Transvaginal ultrasound</u> to evaluate <u>cervix</u>, adnexa, and <u>uterus</u> (e.g., for adnexal adhesions and <u>endometriosis</u>) [[2]](/library/nkd7oJ0)[[4]](/library/5mdiTq0)

* <u>Hysterosalpingography</u> or <u>sonohysterosalpingography</u> to evaluate for:   [[4]](/library/5mdiTq0);  

* <u>Fallopian tube</u> patency and morphology (e.g., tubal occlusion)

* Uterine abnormalities (e.g., <u>septate uterus</u>, <u>submucosal fibroids</u>, <u>intrauterine adhesions</u>)

### Further assessment [[2]](/library/nkd7oJ0)[[3]](/library/yKddQI0)[[4]](/library/5mdiTq0)




Further assessment is typically performed by reproductive <u>endocrinology</u> and may include the following.




* Testing for diminished ovarian reserve, which may show:   [[3]](/library/yKddQI0)[[4]](/library/5mdiTq0)

* ↓ <u>Anti-Müllerian hormone</u> level

* ↑ <u>FSH</u> and <u>estradiol</u> on days 2–4 of <u>the menstrual cycle</u>  [[4]](/library/5mdiTq0)

* ↓ Antral follicle count on <u>transvaginal ultrasound</u>

* <u>Hysteroscopy</u>: for definitive evaluation of intrauterine <u>causes of infertility</u>

* Additional diagnostic studies (e.g., <u>laparoscopy</u> with chromopertubation, <u>MRI</u> <u>pelvis</u>)





> [!TIP]
> Although <u>ovarian reserve testing</u> can predict responsiveness to ovarian stimulation, it does not predict reproductive potential better than the patient's age and should not be performed to evaluate reproductive potential in female individuals without infertility. [[3]](/library/yKddQI0)

---

## Male individuals

### Initial assessment [[9]](/library/R5dlPq0)[[13]](/library/ddWoK40)[[14]](/library/-7dDor0)[[15]](/library/0HdeKr0)




* Perform:

* <u>Physical examination</u>, including <u>penis</u> and <u>testes</u>

* <u>Semen analysis</u>

* Refer to urology if there are abnormal findings on initial evaluation.





### Further assessment [[9]](/library/R5dlPq0)[[13]](/library/ddWoK40)[[14]](/library/-7dDor0)[[15]](/library/0HdeKr0)




Further assessment is typically performed by urology and may include the following.




* <u>FSH</u> and total <u>testosterone</u>, and possibly testicular <u>biopsy</u>: to assess for abnormal <u>spermatogenesis</u> (i.e., rule out <u>obstructive azoospermia</u>)

* Additional endocrine evaluation (e.g., <u>LH</u>, <u>prolactin</u>, <u>TSH</u>): to assess for underlying cause of low total <u>testosterone</u>

* <u>Genetic testing</u> (e.g., <u>karyotyping</u>, <u>Y chromosome microdeletion</u>, <u>cystic fibrosis</u> testing): to assess for genetic conditions associated with <u>male infertility</u> (e.g., <u>Klinefelter syndrome</u>)   [[9]](/library/R5dlPq0)

* Specialized semen testing (e.g., <u>sperm</u> <u>antibody</u> testing, <u>sperm</u> <u>DNA</u> fragmentation): to assess for other impairments of <u>sperm</u> function

* <u>Post-ejaculatory urinalysis</u>: to assess for <u>retrograde ejaculation</u>

* Imaging (e.g., <u>transrectal ultrasonography</u>): to assess for structural causes of <u>obstructive azoospermia</u>





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Antisperm antibodies</u> form when the <u>blood testis barrier</u> is disrupted, usually due to infections or trauma of the male genital tract, and can lead to <u>immobilization</u> and agglutination of <u>sperm</u> or have a spermatoxic effect. [[13]](/library/ddWoK40)[[16]](/library/W6dPPI0)

---

## Management

### Approach [[2]](/library/nkd7oJ0)[[5]](/library/IudYs70)[[9]](/library/R5dlPq0)




* All patients:

* Provide <u>preconception care</u>, including <u>preconception counseling on diet and lifestyle</u>.

* Consider referral to <u>infertility counseling</u> services.

* Patients with <u>anovulation</u>

* Manage underlying conditions, e.g., <u>hyperprolactinemia</u> (with <u>bromocriptine</u>), <u>hypothyroidism</u> (with <u>levothyroxine</u>), and <u>insulin resistance</u> in <u>PCOS</u> (with <u>metformin</u>).

* Patients with <u>eugonadotropic eugonadism</u> (e.g., <u>PCOS</u>): Provide oral <u>ovulation induction</u>.

* Refer female patients to reproductive <u>endocrinology</u> for consideration of <u>medically assisted reproduction</u> if:

* A structural cause of infertility such as tubal disease or uterine lesions is identified (surgical management may also be considered for, e.g., removal of adhesions or <u>leiomyomas</u>)

* No cause for infertility is identified [[8]](/library/OMdIKq0)

* <u>Pregnancy</u> is not achieved after 6 cycles of oral <u>ovulation induction</u> [[2]](/library/nkd7oJ0)

* <u>Assisted reproductive technology</u> is desired

* Refer male patients to urology.





### Ovulation induction [[2]](/library/nkd7oJ0)[[17]](/library/EKd8RI0)




The goal of <u>ovulation induction</u> is to stimulate development of a single <u>dominant follicle</u> in patients with <u>anovulation</u>.  [[17]](/library/EKd8RI0)




* Oral medications

* Indications

* <u>Anovulation</u> with <u>eugonadotropic eugonadism</u> (e.g., <u>PCOS</u>)

* Unexplained infertility [[8]](/library/OMdIKq0)

* Options

* <u>Letrozole</u> (<u>off-label</u>): first-line in <u>PCOS</u> (see “<u>Treatment of PCOS</u>” for details) DOSAGE [[18]](/library/tEdXx70)[[19]](/library/b5XHiA)

* <u>Clomiphene citrate</u> DOSAGE  [[20]](/library/8EdOx70)

* Pulsatile <u>GnRH</u>: may be used for <u>functional hypothalamic amenorrhea</u>  [[21]](/library/JEds970)

* <u>Exogenous</u> <u>gonadotropins</u>

* Indications

* <u>Anovulation</u> due to <u>hypogonadotropic hypogonadism</u>

* Inadequate response to oral agents

* Options: recombinant <u>FSH</u>, <u>LH</u>, and/or <u>hCG</u>





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Ovulation induction</u> increases the risk of <u>multiple pregnancy</u>, and <u>ovulation induction</u> with <u>exogenous</u> <u>gonadotropins</u> increases the risk of <u>ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome</u>. [[17]](/library/EKd8RI0)




### Other forms of <u>medically assisted reproduction</u> [[5]](/library/IudYs70)[[22]](/library/2jdT-p0)




* <u>Intrauterine insemination</u>: an <u>infertility treatment</u> in which washed and concentrated <u>sperm</u> are introduced directly into the <u>uterine cavity</u> at the time of <u>ovulation</u> [[23]](/library/uEdpx70)

* Assisted reproductive technology: infertility treatments involving the in vitro handling of human embryos, or of <u>oocytes</u> together with <u>sperm</u>





#### <u>Assisted reproductive technology</u>




<u>In vitro fertilization</u> may be combined with <u>intracytoplasmic sperm injection</u> and/or the use of donor <u>gametes</u>. [[24]](/library/bLWHwN0)




* In vitro fertilization [[25]](/library/SMdyLq0)

* Multiple <u>oocytes</u> are obtained through ovarian stimulation with <u>exogenous</u> <u>gonadotropins</u>. [[25]](/library/SMdyLq0)

* Transvaginal follicular puncture for <u>oocyte</u> retrieval is performed with <u>ultrasound</u> monitoring.

* <u>Fertilization</u> of <u>gametes</u> occurs extracorporeally.

* Embryos are transferred into the <u>uterus</u>.

* Intracytoplasmic sperm injection: <u>Sperm</u> is injected into an <u>oocyte</u> during <u>in vitro fertilization</u>. [[22]](/library/2jdT-p0)

* <u>Gamete donation</u> [[26]](/library/mMdV6q0)

---

## Complications

Patients who start <u>assisted reproductive technology</u> are at risk of complications related to ovarian stimulation.




### Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (<u>OHSS</u>) [[27]](/library/xXcEZY0)[[28]](/library/Xad9Qo0)




* Definition: a potentially life-threatening complication of <u>ovulation induction</u> or ovarian stimulation with <u>exogenous</u> <u>human chorionic gonadotropin</u> (<u>hCG</u>)

* Pathophysiology

* <u>Exogenous</u> <u>hCG</u> is thought to be responsible for the massive <u>luteinization</u> of the ovarian <u>granulosa cells</u>.

* Formation of multiple <u>ovarian follicles</u> and <u>corpus luteum cysts</u> with rapid ovarian enlargement

* ↑ Release of vasoactive mediators (e.g., <u>VEGF</u>) that induce an increase in <u>capillary</u> permeability and consequent <u>third spacing</u> into the <u>abdominal cavity</u>

* Clinical features: onset between 3 days (early onset) and ≥ 9 days (late onset) after <u>hCG</u> administration

* Abdominal <u>pain</u> and distention

* <u>Nausea</u> and/or <u>vomiting</u>

* Weight gain

* <u>Ascites</u>

* <u>Oliguria</u> or <u>anuria</u>

* <u>Dyspnea</u>

* <u>Pleural effusion</u>

* <u>Syncope</u>

* Venous <u>thrombosis</u>

* Diagnostics

* <u>Laboratory analysis</u>

* <u>CBC</u> (↑ <u>Hct</u>, <u>leukocytosis</u>)

* Serum <u>electrolyte</u> concentrations

* <u>Renal function tests</u>

* <u>Liver function</u> tests

* <u>Transvaginal ultrasound</u>: <u>ascites</u> and ovarian enlargement

* Management

* Mild to moderate <u>OHSS</u> (usually early onset): Manage on an outpatient basis.  

* Limit physical activity.

* <u>Pain management</u> with <u>acetaminophen</u>

* Daily monitoring of body weight (should not increase by > 1 kg/day) and urine output

* Sufficient hydration (1–2 L/day)

* <u>Paracentesis</u> to relieve symptoms of <u>ascites</u>

* Severe <u>OHSS</u> (usually late onset) 

* Hospitalization

* Multidisciplinary management approach: <u>supportive care</u> (e.g., cautious <u>IV fluids</u>), monitoring, and prevention of complications (e.g., prophylactic anticoagulation)

* Complications

* <u>Sepsis</u>

* <u>Thromboembolism</u>

* <u>Pericardial effusion</u>

* <u>Arrhythmias</u>

* <u>Acute respiratory distress syndrome</u>

* <u>Acute kidney injury</u>
